cards.b: Red, yellow, blue; cannot be mixed from other paints.
Orange, green, purple; each is made by mixing two primaries.
A primary mixed with its neighbouring secondary, e.g. red-orange.
Opposites on the wheel; strong contrast, and dull neutrals when mixed.
Neighbours on the wheel; calm, harmonious.
Colour name; lightness or darkness; purity or intensity.
Tint = colour + white; shade = colour + black.
Warm (red, orange, yellow) advance; cool (blue, green) recede.
A thin diluted layer of paint; flat or graded.
A thin transparent layer over a dry layer to deepen colour.
Thick paint where brush or knife marks show; used by Van Gogh.
Opaque, water-based, matte paint good for flat colour and illustration.
Fast-drying plastic-based paint; waterproof when dry; thick or thin.
Scratching through a layer of paint to reveal the layer below.
Colours side by side look more intense; explored by Josef Albers.

short.q: Why avoid adding black to darken colours?
short.model: Black can make colours look dull and dead. A darker colour or the complement gives richer shadows.
points: alternative such as complement or dark blue

short.model: Watercolour is transparent and good for soft washes but hard to correct. Acrylic is opaque or thin, dries fast and can be built thickly with texture.

short.q: How can colour be used to create a focal point?
short.model: Place a small area of a complementary or warm contrasting colour against a cool or neutral background so the eye goes there first.

short.q: Name an artist known for colour and explain one technique.
short.model: Van Gogh used impasto and expressive complementary colour such as blue and orange to create energy.

short.q: Why is selection important when testing paint media?
short.model: You must choose the medium that best suits your idea and explain why, which shows AO2 judgement, not just trying things.
